Everything in `vignette("compare_pms")` assumes you already have two or three
files recorded from the same riding. Getting those files is the part that
actually goes wrong, and most of the ways it goes wrong cannot be repaired
afterwards: a dropped sample is gone, a mid-ride auto-pause cannot be undone,
and a perfectly steady hour contains no evidence about how far apart the head
unit clocks were.

This vignette is the recording protocol. It is short, and following it costs
one extra minute at the start of a ride.

## One meter, many listeners

The constraint that shapes the whole setup is that a power meter broadcasts,
but a recorder records one power source. There is no consumer head unit that
writes two power channels into an ordinary file.

Over ANT+ that is not a problem. ANT+ is a one-to-many broadcast with no
handshake, so a single meter can be picked up by any number of head units at
once, and two head units listening to the same meter do not interfere with each
other. Bluetooth is a connection rather than a broadcast, and classically a
meter accepted one at a time; recent firmware on many meters allows two, but
you cannot rely on it.

The practical rule follows: **pair each meter to its own recorder over ANT+
wherever the meter offers it**, and keep Bluetooth for the one device that has
no ANT+ radio — usually a phone or a computer running Zwift. Do not pair the
same meter to two apps over Bluetooth and hope; the second connection will
either be refused or will drop out intermittently, and intermittent drop-outs
are much harder to spot in the file than a flat refusal.

So two meters need two recorders, and three meters need three. Common
combinations:

| Meters | Recorders |
|---|---|
| Trainer + pedals | Zwift (trainer, over Bluetooth) and a head unit (pedals, over ANT+) |
| Two bike-mounted meters | Two head units, both over ANT+ |
| Three meters | Two head units plus a phone app, or two runs and a bridge meter — see below |

Two head units of the same model are marginally better than two different ones,
because they will resolve and log the broadcast the same way. It is not
important enough to buy one for.

## Settings on each recorder

Three settings matter, and the first two matter a great deal.

**Record every second, not "smart" recording.** Garmin's smart recording writes
a sample only when the numbers change enough, which produces a file with
irregular gaps. `align_rides()` resamples onto a one-second grid and leaves
unrecorded seconds empty, so smart recording thins the series that the
cross-correlation and the per-second differencing both work on. This is the
single most damaging setting on the head unit, and it is on by default on some
units.

**Turn auto-pause off on every recorder.** `align_rides()` estimates one clock
offset per source per run. An auto-pause that triggers on one unit and not the
other — at a junction, or when the trainer drops below the speed threshold —
shifts everything after it by the length of the pause, so the true offset
becomes two different numbers and no single correction fixes both. A stopped
period recorded as zeros is fine; the coasting seconds are dropped from the
agreement anyway.

**Let the clocks set themselves.** Head units take their clock from GPS, and
two units that both have a fix will usually be within a second or two of each
other. A unit ridden indoors without a fix can be minutes out, and
`align_rides()` only searches ±30 seconds by default. If you ride indoors, take
each unit outside for a minute before you start, or raise `max_offset`.

Beyond that: start and stop both recorders as close together as you can manage,
and if you are in a busy gym, keep each head unit near its meter, since ANT+
drop-outs from a crowded band show up as missing seconds in one file only.

## Calibrating before you start

Do a zero offset on every meter, following the manufacturer's instructions,
immediately before each run and after a few minutes of easy pedalling — most
meters drift with temperature, and a meter that has been in a cold garage will
read differently over the first ten minutes than it does later.

Do not re-zero one meter mid-ride. A step change in one series and not the
other is not something the analysis models: it will average the before and
after into a single bias, and the limits of agreement will widen without any
indication of why.

## What to actually ride

Two things the analysis needs pull in opposite directions, and this is the part
worth planning.

**The alignment needs features.** `align_rides()` recovers each clock offset by
sliding one power trace against another and taking the offset with the highest
correlation. A block at constant power correlates about equally well at every
offset, so there is no peak to find, and `check_alignment()` returns
`unresolved`, forces the offset to zero and warns. That is the honest answer,
but it means a clean ERG session — the most controlled ride you can do — is the
worst possible ride for establishing what the offset was.

**The by-level comparison needs coverage.** `agreement_by_level()` bins seconds
by the mean of the two readings, so a bin only exists if you spent time there.
Two hundred seconds at 250 W tells you about the meters at 250 W and nothing
about them at 400 W.

So structure the run in two parts.

*Start with a synchronisation block.* Four to six sharp surges — eight to ten
seconds well above your average for the day — each separated by about thirty
seconds of soft pedalling or, better, complete coasting. Coast-to-power
transitions are the sharpest edges available and are exactly what the
cross-correlation locks onto. The coasting seconds are then dropped from the
agreement calculation, so this block costs you nothing in the comparison. It
takes about four minutes.

*Then ride steps.* Choose five or six targets spanning the range you care about
— something like 55, 70, 85, 100 and 110 per cent of FTP — and hold each for
four to five minutes. Steps are better than a ramp: a ramp sweeps every bin but
leaves each one with a handful of transient seconds, recorded while both meters
were still responding to a change, and meters respond at different speeds. Each
step instead fills one or two bins with a few hundred stable seconds, and the
transitions between steps populate the bins in between.

*Repeat the synchronisation block at the end* if the session is longer than an
hour. It is not needed for the alignment, but it lets you check for clock drift:
align the first ten minutes and the last ten minutes separately, and if the two
offsets differ, one unit's clock moved during the ride and a single constant
correction is not enough for that file.

## Comparing a trainer against a bike-mounted meter

A crank, spider or pedal meter measures power at the pedals; a trainer or hub
measures it after the chain has been through the drivetrain. The difference is
real, typically two to four per cent, and it is not disagreement between the
meters — it is the transmission.

Nothing in the package knows this. `power_agreement()` will report a `gain_pc`
of a few per cent for a pair of perfectly accurate devices in that
configuration, so read the number net of an expected drivetrain loss rather
than as pure measurement error. A clean drivetrain in a straight chainline sits
at the low end of the range and a worn one at the high end, which is itself a
reason not to try to pin the figure down too precisely.

Two bike-mounted meters do not have this problem, and pedals against a
crank-based meter differ by only the bottom-bracket bearings, which is small
enough to ignore.

## Three meters and two recorders

If you have three meters but can only record two at a time, ride two sessions
with one meter common to both: run one carries A and B, run two carries B and
C. B is the bridge, and `chain_sources()` gets A against C from the two gains
relative to B.

That comparison rests on B having read identically on both days, which the ride
files cannot test, so the protocol is about protecting the assumption:

- Ride the two runs as close together as you can — back to back on the same day
  is much better than a week apart.
- Change nothing about B in between. No reinstallation, no battery change, no
  firmware update, no crank-length or scale-factor edits.
- Cover the same power range in both runs. Use the same step targets, not just
  a similar overall effort. A gain estimated at endurance pace in one run and
  at threshold in the other is not really the same quantity.
- Keep the conditions comparable, particularly temperature.

`chain_report()` reports what can be checked — the overlap in power range
between the runs — and states the assumption in the output. Keep that statement
wherever the numbers go.

## Getting the files out and named

Export from each device as FIT where you can. GPX works, but Strava's GPX
export only carries power that a meter actually recorded: power Strava
estimated from speed and gradient is not in the file, so a ride recorded
without a meter arrives with no power channel at all, which is an error rather
than a column of `NA`.

Name each file `<run>_<source>`, where the run is the session and the source is
the meter:

```
rides/
  run1_kickr.fit
  run1_assioma.fit
  run2_assioma.fit
  run2_quarq.fit
```

Then `ride_spec_from_names()` builds the table `read_rides()` wants, and a
filename that does not split cleanly is an error rather than a silently
mislabelled ride.

```{r pipeline}
library(cyclingpower)

aligned <- list.files("rides", full.names = TRUE) |>
  ride_spec_from_names() |>
  read_rides() |>
  align_rides()
```

## Checking that the recording worked

Three checks before you trust anything downstream, all worth doing while you
could still repeat the ride.

The alignment resolved:

```{r check-alignment}
alignment_report(aligned)
```

Every source should have `status` of `aligned`, and the `offset` should be a
few seconds. An `unresolved` status means the synchronisation block was too
soft or is missing; a large correlation with a large offset means the clocks
really were far apart, which is fine. A low correlation on a ride you know had
surges in it usually means the two files are not the same session.

The bins are populated:

```{r check-coverage}
agreement_by_level(aligned) |>
  dplyr::select(pair, level, seconds, bias_w)
```

The `seconds` column is there to be read. A bin resting on twenty seconds is
not evidence of anything, and the steps are what fill the bins you care about.

And, for a chained comparison, that the two runs actually covered comparable
ground:

```{r check-chain}
chain_report(chain_sources(aligned))$coverage
```

## The short version

- One recorder per meter; ANT+ where the meter offers it.
- One-second recording, auto-pause off, clocks set from GPS.
- Zero every meter after a warm-up, immediately before the run.
- Open with four to six coast-to-sprint surges so the alignment has something
  to lock onto.
- Then five or six steady steps across the range you want to report on.
- Expect a trainer to read two to four per cent below a pedal or crank meter.
- Name the files `<run>_<source>` and check `alignment_report()` first.
